content: Human females exhibit a phenomenon known as concealed ovulation or hidden estrus. Unlike many other female animals, who display clear and observable signs when they are in estrus or in heat, human females show very few external indicators of fertility. For example, in species such as baboons and bonobos, there is noticeable swelling and redness of the genitalia during estrus, while members of the feline family release pheromones to signal their reproductive state. In contrast, it is challenging to determine whether a woman is ovulating based solely on external physical signs. Humans are unique among mammals in that they lack obvious, visible manifestations of ovulation. Some researchers, however, argue that the extended estrus period observed in bonobos—where reproductive-age females are in heat for approximately 75% of their menstrual cycle—may serve a similar function to the absence of a distinct heat period in human females. While women can be trained to recognize their own ovulation through methods such as fertility awareness, the ability of men to detect ovulation in women remains a topic of significant debate. At least one recent study has suggested that men are more likely to initiate sexual activity with women who are fertile, whereas another study has found that male-initiated sexual activity occurs at a consistent rate throughout the menstrual cycle. One group of researchers has proposed that the evolution of concealed ovulation and menstruation played a critical role in the development of symbolic culture in early human societies.
